name: Hangi
historicNote: Hangi is a traditional Maori method of cooking food in an earth oven, using stones heated in a pit fire to steam meat and vegetables underground for several hours. It remains central to communal occasions across Aotearoa New Zealand - hui (gatherings), tangihanga (funeral rites), and celebrations - where preparing and sharing a hangi is as much a social and cultural act as it is a cooking technique.
whenEaten: Marae gatherings, weddings, and other large Maori community occasions where feeding everyone from one shared earth oven is part of the occasion itself.
shortDescription: Meat and root vegetables slow-steamed for hours in an underground pit over volcanic stones, wrapped in leaves and cloth.
headnote: A real hangi is dug and built in the ground and is genuinely a group effort, not a solo weeknight recipe - this version keeps the same heated-stones-and-steam principle but scales it down to a large backyard pit, which is how many home cooks in New Zealand still do it outside marae settings.
equipment: A dug earth pit, at least 1m deep
River stones or volcanic rock that can withstand direct fire without cracking
Wire baskets to hold the food, or traditional leaf wrapping
Wet sacking or cloth and soil to seal the pit
miseEnPlace: Dig the pit and gather enough stones the day before if possible
Peel and prepare all root vegetables so they go into the pit at the same time as the meat
Soak the sacking or cloth used to seal the pit so it holds steam rather than burning

items.name: salt
items.prepNote: for seasoning the meat before wrapping

steps.title: Heat the stones
steps.instruction: Build a large fire over the stones in the pit and burn it down until the stones are white-hot and the fire has mostly burned to embers.

heat.flameNote: a large, sustained wood fire built directly on top of the stones

steps.technique: Heating the stones themselves is what stores enough heat to steam-cook everything for hours underground
steps.visualCue: Stones glow faintly and show a light coating of white ash, with no large flames left
steps.commonMistake: Using stones that hold moisture (like some river stones) risks them cracking or exploding under intense heat - use stones known to be safe for fire

steps.title: Rake the embers and place the food
steps.instruction: Rake back the embers, seasoning {0001} and {0002} with {0007}, and lower the wire baskets holding the meat directly onto the hot stones, with {0003}, {0004}, {0005}, and {0006} arranged around and above.
steps.technique: Meat sits closest to the hottest stones since it needs the most sustained heat; vegetables steam above it
steps.visualCue: Baskets sit flat and stable directly on the stones with no gaps for heat to escape unevenly
steps.commonMistake: Working too slowly here lets the stones cool before the pit is sealed

steps.title: Seal the pit
steps.instruction: Cover the food completely with wet sacking or cloth, then shovel soil over the top to seal in the steam entirely.
steps.technique: A fully airtight earth seal is what turns the stones' stored heat and the food's own moisture into steam
steps.visualCue: No steam is visibly escaping anywhere around the mound of soil
steps.commonMistake: An incomplete seal lets steam vent out, leaving the food undercooked after the wait

steps.title: Steam underground
steps.instruction: Leave the sealed pit completely undisturbed.

heat.flameNote: no active fire - the stored heat in the stones does the cooking

steps.technique: Long, even steam-cooking under an airtight earth seal tenderizes large cuts of meat without any direct fire contact
steps.visualCue: Ground above the pit stays warm to the touch throughout
steps.commonMistake: Digging the pit open early to check loses the steam and stalls the cook - trust the timing

chefTips: Everyone helping with a hangi typically has one job - fire, food prep, or digging - since the timing across all of it needs to line up closely
Whole, unpeeled kumara and potatoes hold their shape and moisture better through the long steam than cut pieces
donenessSummary: Meat pulls easily from the bone and root vegetables are fully soft all the way through when pierced.
platingNote: Uncover the pit and lift the baskets out together, serving the meat and vegetables straight from the hangi while everyone gathers around.
storageNote: Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours of uncovering the pit; use within 3 days.

substitutions.impact: Similarly tender after the long steam, with a heavier, beefier flavour

regionalVariations: Coastal hangi sometimes include fish or shellfish added later in the cook, since they need far less time than the meat and root vegetables
